items.stem: The Cold War policy of containment committed the United States to resisting communist expansion. Which post–Cold War American action shows the strongest continuity with that tradition?
options: (A) The adoption of strict isolationism, the closing of every overseas base, and the withdrawal of all American forces to within national borders.
(B) The abolition of the armed forces after 1991.
(C) A refusal to participate in any international coalition or alliance.
(D) Leading coalitions against aggression (Iraq in Kuwait) and atrocities (the Balkans), extending intervention to new causes.
items.explanation: Containment built the machinery and the mindset: America as the organizer of coalitions against aggression. After 1991 the enemy changed but the habit persisted — Washington still assembled alliances and projected force, now in the name of international order rather than anti-communism.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The United States did not adopt isolationism; the 1990s were an interventionist decade with bases retained worldwide.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The armed forces were reduced but remained the world's largest and most capable military.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The Gulf War coalition is the textbook counterexample: dozens of nations acting together under American leadership.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It identifies the continuity: the institutional habit of American-led collective action, repurposed from containing communism to policing the post–Cold War order.

items.stem: 'The Soviet Union did not fall to American arms. It fell because its economy could not feed its people or match its rivals, and because its subject peoples wanted out.' — original composition in the style of 1991 news analysis. A historian would find this passage most useful as evidence for which interpretation of the Soviet collapse?

stimulus.text: The Soviet Union did not fall to American arms. It fell because its economy could not feed its people or match its rivals, and because its subject peoples wanted out. — Original composition in the style of 1991 news analysis.

options: (A) The internal-decay interpretation: economic failure and nationalist secession as the primary drivers of collapse.
(B) The interpretation that American military invasion caused the collapse.
(C) The interpretation that Gorbachev's reforms fully succeeded in saving the Soviet system, preserving the union intact into the twenty-first century.
(D) The interpretation that the Soviet economy was outperforming the American economy in 1991.
items.explanation: The passage explicitly demotes American arms ('did not fall to American arms') and promotes two internal causes: an economy that could not deliver and subject peoples demanding independence. That is the internal-decay school in miniature — useful to a historian mapping the debate's positions, though not proof the school is right.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The passage's two named causes — economic failure and nationalist secession — are exactly the internal-decay interpretation's pillars.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The passage's first sentence explicitly rejects invasion as the cause.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The passage describes a system that fell, not one saved; Gorbachev's reforms appear here as context for failure, not success.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The passage says the Soviet economy 'could not feed its people or match its rivals' — the opposite of outperforming America.

items.fact_source: u9.md §What the exam tests here — 'internal Soviet decay and Gorbachev's reforms' as required causes

items.stem: The chart shows crude oil prices collapsing in the mid-1980s. A historian comparing the American and Soviet systems notes that the United States weathered this price swing while the USSR was devastated by it. What systemic difference best explains the contrast?

chart_spec.title: Crude Oil Prices, 1973–1990 (nominal dollars per barrel)
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures; the 1980s oil-price collapse that squeezed Soviet export revenues, an internal pressure on the USSR alongside the factors in u9.md §What the exam tests here ('internal Soviet decay').

options: (A) The United States produced no oil at all, so the price change did not affect its economy.
(B) America's flexible market economy absorbed the shock; the Soviet command economy depended on oil exports and could not adapt.
(C) The Soviet Union's economy was far more diversified and flexible than America's, so it absorbed the price shock easily.
(D) Oil prices did not actually change in the 1980s, according to the chart.
items.explanation: A market economy reallocates: cheap oil hurt Texas producers but helped every American consumer and manufacturer, with the gains outweighing the losses. The Soviet system could not reallocate — its rigid planning and dependence on a single export for foreign earnings turned the same price swing into a fiscal catastrophe.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The United States was a major oil producer; the price fall hurt domestic producers even as it helped consumers — the point is that the system absorbed both effects.
option_explanations.B: Correct. It names the systemic contrast the comparison requires: flexibility and diversification versus rigidity and single-commodity dependence.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The Soviet economy was far less diversified in its foreign earnings; oil and gas dominated its hard-currency income.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The chart shows a fall from $35.50 to the mid-$20s — a large change, not stability.

items.fact_source: u9.md §What the exam tests here — 'internal Soviet decay' as a required cause of the Cold War's end

items.stem: The chart shows crude oil prices falling by roughly a third in the mid-1980s. How did this price collapse compound the cost of the Soviet war in Afghanistan (1979–1989)?

chart_spec.title: Crude Oil Prices, 1973–1990 (nominal dollars per barrel)
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures; the 1980s oil-price collapse that squeezed Soviet export revenues, an internal pressure on the USSR alongside the factors in u9.md §What the exam tests here ('internal Soviet decay').

options: (A) The price collapse made the war cheaper for Moscow, since armies run on oil.
(B) Afghanistan paid the Soviet Union in regular oil shipments, making the long war profitable for Moscow overall.
(C) Falling oil revenues left Moscow less able to afford the stalemated war, deepening the 'bleeding wound.'
(D) The war ended in 1980, before prices fell, so the two were unrelated.
items.explanation: Gorbachev himself called Afghanistan a 'bleeding wound.' The war consumed money, men, and morale for a decade; when the oil-price collapse simultaneously drained the revenue that funded the Soviet state, the combination of a costly stalemate abroad and a fiscal crisis at home made withdrawal the only rational choice — completed in 1989.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Cheaper oil did not offset the war's costs; the revenue lost on exports dwarfed any savings on fuel, and the war's expense was overwhelmingly in men and materiel.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Afghanistan did not pay Moscow in oil; the war was a pure drain on Soviet resources.
option_explanations.C: Correct. It connects the chart's revenue shock to the war's fiscal burden, showing how two pressures multiplied each other.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The Soviets withdrew in 1989, well after the mid-1980s price collapse; the timing overlaps directly.

items.stem: The chart shows U.S. military spending nearly doubling between 1980 and 1985. A student claims that the Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI) alone ended the Cold War. Which rebuttal is strongest?

chart_spec.title: U.S. Military Spending, 1980–1990 (nominal)
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures; the Reagan-era military buildup described in u9.md §The story ('spending massively on the military abroad').

options: (A) SDI was fully deployed in 1985, and its orbital lasers destroyed the entire Soviet nuclear arsenal within months.
(B) Soviet leaders never heard of SDI, so it could not have affected their decisions.
(C) SDI single-handedly caused the Berlin Wall to fall in 1989.
(D) SDI was never built and ended nothing by itself; the chart's broad buildup was only one cause among many.
items.explanation: The single-program theory fails twice: SDI never moved beyond research, so it could not have 'ended' anything mechanically, and the chart shows the pressure was economy-wide across the defense budget, not a single wonder weapon. The review's multi-causal rule then finishes the rebuttal: internal Soviet decay and Gorbachev's reforms were equally necessary.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. SDI was never deployed; no space-based lasers ever destroyed anything.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Soviet leaders were well aware of SDI and alarmed by it; the program's psychological pressure was real even though the system was not.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The Wall fell because of Eastern European revolutions and Gorbachev's non-intervention, not because of an undeployed missile-defense concept.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It corrects the factual error (never built), widens the lens to the full buildup the chart documents, and applies the review's multi-causal standard.

items.fact_source: u9.md §Key terms — SDI: 'pressured the Soviets and spurred arms-control talks'; §What the exam tests here — multi-causal answers, 'not single-hero stories'

items.stem: German reunification in 1990 mattered beyond Germany itself for which reason?
options: (A) It erased the Cold War's central dividing line in Europe, confirming that the postwar order was over.
(B) It restored the German monarchy that had ruled before 1918.
(C) It caused the United States to withdraw from NATO immediately after reunification, ending the American commitment to Europe.
(D) It had no significance outside Germany's own borders.
items.explanation: Divided Germany was the Cold War's physical embodiment: the line where the two blocs faced each other. Reunification — achieved peacefully and inside NATO — meant the division of Europe itself was ending, not just one country's internal arrangement.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It states the wider significance: reunification was the continent's reunification in miniature, the moment the Iron Curtain's central front dissolved.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Reunification created no monarchy; the united Germany remained the democratic Federal Republic.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The United States stayed in NATO, and reunified Germany stayed in it too — a key condition Moscow reluctantly accepted.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Few events of 1990 mattered more internationally; it redrew Europe's map and confirmed the Cold War's end.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — 'the Berlin Wall fell in November 1989, Germany reunified, and the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991'

items.stem: NATO survived the Cold War while the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact dissolved. Which explanation best accounts for NATO's persistence?
options: (A) NATO was abolished in 1991 along with the Warsaw Pact.
(B) NATO was a voluntary alliance and its members kept it; the Warsaw Pact was imposed by Moscow and died with Soviet power.
(C) The Soviet Union joined NATO in 1992, keeping the alliance alive.
(D) NATO persisted because its members were legally forbidden from ever leaving the alliance under the treaty's terms.
items.explanation: Alliances held together by consent outlast those held together by coercion. NATO members — democracies that had joined voluntarily — found continued value in the alliance for the Balkans and beyond; the Warsaw Pact, an instrument of Soviet domination, disintegrated the moment Moscow stopped enforcing it.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. NATO was not abolished; it remains active decades after the Cold War's end.
option_explanations.B: Correct. It identifies the structural difference: voluntary alliance versus imposed bloc, which explains their different fates.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The Soviet Union dissolved in 1991 and never joined NATO; Russia's later relationship with the alliance was adversarial.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. NATO's treaty permits withdrawal; members stayed because they judged membership useful, not because exit was barred.

items.fact_source: u9.md §Key terms — End of the Cold War: 'the 1989–1991 collapse of Soviet power in Eastern Europe and the USSR's dissolution, leaving the U.S. the sole superpower'

items.stem: President George H. W. Bush's management of the Cold War's end is often praised by historians for which quality?
options: (A) Rushing to humiliate the Soviet leadership as thoroughly as possible.
(B) Refusing all dealings with Gorbachev throughout the crisis, boycotting every summit, call, and negotiation entirely.
(C) Cautious stewardship: backing reunification in NATO without humiliating Moscow, lest hardliners gain strength.
(D) Ordering an American invasion of Eastern Europe in 1990.
items.explanation: Bush understood that a cornered nuclear superpower was dangerous. He pressed American advantages — reunified Germany in NATO — but gave Gorbachev face-saving cooperation, economic aid discussions, and partnership rhetoric, denying Soviet hardliners the provocation that could have justified a crackdown or coup attempt.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Humiliation was what Bush deliberately avoided; triumphalism, he feared, would strengthen the Kremlin's hardliners.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Bush dealt with Gorbachev extensively, meeting him at summits including Malta in 1989.
option_explanations.C: Correct. It describes the actual stewardship: firm on Western goals, careful about Soviet dignity — the prudence historians credit for the Cold War's peaceful end.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. No such invasion occurred or was contemplated; American policy worked through diplomacy, not force, in Eastern Europe.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — Cold War endgame 1989–1991; Bush's 'new world order' moment

items.stem: Unlike the two World Wars, the Cold War ended without a formal peace treaty or settlement conference. What consequence followed from that difference?
options: (A) The Cold War never actually ended, since only treaties can end wars.
(B) No postwar rules were agreed, so NATO's role and Russia's place stayed unsettled — the 'failure to build a new consensus.'
(C) The United States and Russia became close allies immediately after 1991, with no disagreements between them on any issue whatsoever.
(D) All nuclear weapons were automatically abolished when the Soviet Union dissolved.
items.explanation: Versailles and Yalta wrote the rules of their postwar worlds, however imperfectly. The Cold War just... stopped, with the loser dissolving rather than surrendering. Nothing settled whether NATO should expand, what Russia's sphere included, or what the 'new world order' meant — ambiguities that haunted the decades after, exactly the review's through-line.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Wars can end through collapse and dissolution without treaties; the Cold War's end in 1991 is not seriously disputed.
option_explanations.B: Correct. It connects the missing settlement to the review's central theme: the end of the old consensus without a new one to replace it.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. U.S.-Russian relations were cooperative briefly, then deteriorated sharply; no close alliance resulted.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Russia inherited the Soviet nuclear arsenal; disarmament required separate treaties and remained incomplete.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — 'The through-line of the whole period is the end of the Cold War consensus about America's role in the world — and the failure, so far, to build a new one'

items.stem: The review says 'the 1990s felt like a victory lap.' The chart shows the federal budget moving from a $290 billion deficit in 1992 to a $236 billion surplus in 2000. Which element of the 'victory lap' does the chart document?

chart_spec.title: Federal Budget Deficit (+) / Surplus (−), 1980–2000
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures; Clinton-era surpluses per u9.md §The story (Clinton 'presided over budget surpluses').

options: (A) The return to budget surpluses amid the long 1990s expansion — a fiscal turnaround that reinforced the era's confidence.
(B) The elimination of all federal spending by the year 2000.
(C) A deficit that grew larger in every single year of the 1990s without exception, reaching new records annually.
(D) The chart shows the 1990s were a period of economic depression.
items.explanation: The chart's swing from deep deficit to surplus was the fiscal face of the 1990s boom: the budget deals of 1990 and 1993 plus the tech-driven expansion filled the Treasury. Surpluses let Clinton claim the era's prosperity as policy vindication — part of what made the decade feel like a victory lap.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It reads the chart's 1992–2000 swing accurately and ties it to the expansion and confidence the review describes.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. A surplus means revenues exceeded spending, not that spending was eliminated; federal spending remained enormous.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The chart shows the deficit shrinking after 1992 and turning into surplus by 1998 — the opposite trajectory.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The 1990s brought the longest expansion on record to that point, not a depression; the chart's surpluses reflect boom-time revenues.
